stories.headline: Nepal-Tibet floods leave hundreds dead and thousands missing as a new upstream lake threatens further disaster

sources.body:
Federation says it fears death toll of nearly 600 will continue to rise as rescuers reach cut-off areas

Visual guide: how the deadly flooding unfolded

Tell us: have you been affected by the flash floods?

The Red Cross has said at least 93,000 people may have been affected by Wednesday’s flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border, which have killed nearly 600 people, left another 1,900 missing, and triggered a huge rescue operation that is being hampered by fears of new flooding.

The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), the world’s largest humanitarian network, said it feared the death toll would continue to rise as some of the hardest-hit areas remained inaccessible after roads and bridges were destroyed by the torrents.

“The trauma of this event is enormous,” David Fisher, the IFRC head of delegation for Nepal , said on Friday.

“Thousands of homes have been destroyed or suffered significant damage. We believe that at least 93,000 people have been affected and are in great need. The death toll is very high and unfortunately likely to continue to rise.”

The deadly floods occurred on Wednesday morning after an enormous section ⁠of a glacier in the Himalayas broke loose and crashed on to the valley floor in Nepal’s Langtang national park, unleashing a massive surge of water, mud, rock and ice that thundered down rivers and valleys. The resulting floods obliterated villages and destroyed power stations, roads and bridges.

Nepal’s steep slopes and the lush valleys below are especially vulnerable to flooding and landslides, and extreme weather events, such as intense monsoons, and melting glaciers have become more common because of warming due to human-caused climate change.

“The damage is just incredible,” Lila Pieters Yahia, the UN resident coordinator for Nepal, said on Friday, adding that more than 40 bridges had been destroyed or badly damaged and “over 40km of road completely destroyed”.

By Friday afternoon, the death toll stood at 584 people: 579 in Nepal and five across the border in Tibet, China. Authorities in Nepal said 1,942 people were still missing , including hundreds of foreign nationals who were in the area to work, trek with guides or make a pilgrimage.

Rescue teams have reported finding bodies hundreds of miles downstream from the disaster zone in the Chitwan district of Nepal, near the Indian border. Dozens of injured people were transported to Kathmandu for advanced medical care and more than 100 people were rescued by Nepali army personnel in helicopters.

Rescuers were forced to suspend operations on Friday morning after a dam of debris overflowed on Friday, increasing the risk of further flooding. Residents in Nepal’s Rasuwa district, on the border with Tibet, were seen rushing up hillsides to escape a possible surge in the river, ⁠according to witnesses.

The Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported that a lake formed by piles of debris from the mudslide had begun overflowing on Friday, sending water towards the area where rescue teams were headed, and forcing a brief pause in operations.
sources.headline: At least 93,000 ‘in great need’ after Nepal-Tibet flash floods, says Red Cross

sources.body:
Glacier collapse in Nepal triggered flash floods, mudslides and a barrier lake where a landslide dammed the river.

How a glacial collapse caused Nepal’s catastrophic floods

Two days after a glacier collapse sent a catastrophic flood roaring through parts of Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday, a newly formed river has broken the banks, and a renewed flood threat is looming.

The river breach on Friday halted rescue operations in the area after flash floods and mudslides caused by glacial collapse from the Himalayas led to 469 confirmed deaths. More than 1,000 people remain missing across Nepal and China’s Tibet.

A lake has formed by the buildup of debris at the border of Nepal and China at the flood site, and as it continues to rise, it increases the flood risk.

On Friday, officials in Nepal’s Rasuwa district said they had been notified that the barrier lake had begun to overflow.

“We can see that the level of water in the river is rising,” Narendra Pariyar, Rasuwa’s most senior official, said.

He added that it is currently unclear how high the water level is. “We do not know how big it is and how high is its water level. We can see that the level of water in the river is rising.”

Scientists say this disaster has created not one but two new lakes. One has formed high up near the glacier, where meltwater is now trapped.

The other, much larger and more dangerous lake sits on a river in Nepal, where a huge landslide blocked the valley and dammed the river.

Nepali and Chinese authorities warned on Thursday that the lower lake had formed due to the buildup of debris at the site of the flood.

The lake is rising in level, which means it can burst, Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) warned.

Chinese authorities said they have mobilised an engineering team of eight members to carry out aerial surveys and 3D modelling of the barrier lake, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported on Friday.

However, there are challenges when it comes to accessing the site.

“After the glacier collapse created the lake, many isolated cliffs and steep cliffs appeared along it,” one of the engineers, Chen Hanxiao, told CCTV on Thursday evening.

The lake is near the confluence of the Chhochen Khola and Purepu Tsangpo rivers on the Lhende river system in Nepal.

It is flowing upstream of the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers that carry water south towards Kathmandu, The Kathmandu Post reported.

The glacial collapse which led to the Wednesday flash floods also caused mudslides, pushing rock, ice, mud and debris into river systems.

“The new lake appears to be an avalanche-induced barrier lake. The ice-rock avalanche deposited a huge volume of rock, ice and debris in the river valley, blocking or severely constricting the drainage,” Pawan Bhattarai, assistant professor at the civil engineering department of Nepal’s Kathmandu-based Tribhuvan University, told Al Jazeera.

“Water then accumulated behind this natural barrier, forming the lake. Satellite imagery and even some Chinese media reports has confirmed the barrier lake.”
sources.headline: Why Nepal faces another flood threat from a new lake on China border

sources.body: New satellite imagery and video analysis show the deadly Nepal floods began when part of a glacier near the Chinese border collapsed, triggering a debris flow that raced downstream at up to 150 km/h and devastated communities over more than 80 kilometres. Scientists are still piecing together the exact sequence of events, while authorities warn the disaster may not be over as a newly formed lake upstream has started to overflow.
sources.headline: Nepal flood disaster reconstructed minute by minute

sources.body:
Many of the US president’s goals remain unfulfilled, despite claims of victory.

It has been six months since February 28, when the US and Israel shocked the world by launching missile strikes on Iran, killing Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and several senior Iranian officials in Tehran, as well as scores of children in a school in Minab, southern Iran.

US President Donald Trump then claimed the conflict would only last “four to five weeks”.

In the months since, the war has erupted on several other fronts, reaching as far as the Caspian Sea. It has triggered a global oil supply crisis as the US and Iran battle for control of the strategic Strait of Hormuz, through which more than one-fifth of oil and natural gas cargo transited.

And it has resulted in an estimated 8,000-10,000 deaths, as well as tens of thousands of injuries.

The conflict is also realigning the global order, experts say, as new alliances form and dominant ones show signs of crumbling.

The US’s goals were not initially clear: officials first claimed the strikes were carried out in preemptive self-defence.

According to demands presented on the eve of the war, and a jumble of sometimes contradictory statements from Trump and senior US defence officials, they include the following:

Despite Trump’s claim that the US had “obliterated” Iran’s nuclear capabilities when it joined in at the end of Israel’s 12-day war on Iran in June 2025, the US and Israel again claimed in February that Tehran was just weeks away from developing nuclear weapons.

Repeated strikes on Iran’s nuclear sites during the war have likely caused vast damage to the facilities, but it is believed Tehran still possesses 440kg of highly enriched uranium, which could be used to make a weapon.

The Trump administration wanted Iran to hand over this stock to the US and to commit to zero enrichment of uranium going forward. Iran refused to do this, although at one point appeared open to the possibility of handing the stock over to a third country. Iran also insisted on retaining the capacity to develop a nuclear power programme, which requires much lower levels of uranium enrichment.

Later, Trump briefly floated the idea of US troops retrieving the stock by force – a potentially dangerous mission.

In the June 17 memorandum of understanding (MoU) signed by both sides, Iran agreed not to pursue a nuclear weapon – something it had always pledged anyway. The MoU unravelled as its vague wording led to disagreements about what it actually stipulated.

Clark Summers, a US military veteran and professor at Belmont Abbey College in North Carolina, said the US “can rightly assert that these ends have been achieved. Although for how long before Iran can rebuild is difficult to assess.”

But Iranian expert and professor at the Australian National University (ANU), Alam Saleh, disagreed, and noted that Iran’s nuclear power programme is still intact. “The US lost even before the war,” he said, adding that the effort also shows that Washington failed in last year’s 12-day war.
sources.headline: After six months of war, what have US, Iran gained and lost?

stories.headline: Gaza ceasefire risks collapse, Board of Peace envoy warns

sources.body:
In an interview with Al Jazeera, Nicolay Mladenov says that a return to war would be ‘devastating’.

The failure of both sides to adhere to the roadmap for peace “threatens a collapse of the ceasefire in Gaza”, Nikolay Mladenov, the high representative for the Board of Peace, has warned in an interview with Al Jazeera.

There is “no better alternative to the current plan”, Mladenov said on Thursday, adding that the “return to war would be devastating”.

His warning was “directed at both the Palestinian and Israeli sides”, he said, at a time when the besieged Strip is witnessing continued Israeli raids and attacks.

Mladenov stressed that any retreat from the commitments of the roadmap will negatively affect overall security and humanitarian arrangements in Palestine, which may return the region to a spiral of violence with dire consequences.

The Board of Peace has “determined the mechanism for deploying the International Stabilization Force [ISF] and its deployment locations in the Gaza Strip,” he said, noting that Morocco agreed to take part, though Turkiye will not participate after Israel vetoed Ankara’s involvement.

He added that the force’s “advance elements should arrive in the Gaza Strip soon”.

On reconstruction, Mladenov told Al Jazeera that the Board has received pledges worth $7bn, while crediting Qatar, Egypt and Turkiye with playing “an important role” in advancing the agreement with Hamas.

He noted talks with Israel on increasing humanitarian aid are “good”, while expressing hope that a Palestinian national committee would “assume its responsibilities in the Gaza Strip soon”.

The National Committee for the Administration of Gaza is a proposed technocratic, non-factional authority tasked with running day-to-day civil affairs. It is designed to manage public services and coordinate local reconstruction independently of Hamas and other political factions.

Mladenov first proposed a 15-point roadmap on May 21, covering reconstruction, disarmament of Palestinian armed groups, an Israeli gradual withdrawal, and the ISF’s mandate, alongside restructuring Gaza’s police.

The Board of Peace announced on July 31 that it had reached an agreement on the roadmap for the ceasefire’s next phase. Hamas said it had approved it and called on Israel to be held to its implementation.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu subsequently rejected the plan, denying reports that his government had agreed to allow the international troops into Gaza at all. This leaves the roadmap’s status publicly contested even as the US and the Board of Peace said it’s the only viable path forward.

On the ground, Israel’s violations of the ceasefire have continued unabated. Since the ceasefire took effect in October 2025, 1,303 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli fire, and 4,336 more were wounded, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.

The overall toll from Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza since October 2023 stands at 73,438 killed and 174,447 wounded, the ministry said.

Mladenov’s warning also comes amid renewed, if uncertain, diplomatic movement.
sources.headline: Board of Peace envoy Mladenov warns Gaza ceasefire risks ‘collapse’

Efforts to rebuild domestic food production face severe challenges and have come at deadly cost

A s Gaza’s population of 2.1 million has been hemmed into an ever smaller slice of the territory, farmers are using every last remaining patch of unspoiled earth, no matter how tiny, in their struggle to survive.

With severe shortages of water, fertiliser and pesticide, and with more than 80% of greenhouses ruined, it has taken inventiveness and determination to clear land of debris and coax new seedlings into life. Moreover, venturing out into the open to tend to plants can be deadly.

Saqer Abu Rabee’s eldest son and brother were killed while at work growing food for their communities on their small agricultural plots in Beit Lahiya in northern Gaza. His son Yousef was 24 when he was killed by a drone-fired missile in October 2024. Abu Rabee was working in the fields 10 metres from his son when it happened.

“The missile was aimed directly at him and I have no doubt that he was the intended target,” Abu Rabee said. Yousef was well known locally as the driving force behind a collective first called We’ll Plant It and now simply Our Land, which brought together volunteers and encouraged farmers to go back to the land to restore agriculture in the area.

“They decided to target him directly,” said Abu Rabee, who stressed his son had no political affiliations. “Before his death, we received daily threats from the Israeli army. They shelled our area every day three or four times while I was working alongside the labourers.”

Abu Rabee’s brother Bilal was killed on 2 July after he went to retrieve some agricultural supplies from a destroyed building. His death came nine months into a partial ceasefire during which Israeli forces have killed more than 1,200 Palestinians. Abu Rabee is convinced farmers have become prime targets because of their role in sustaining Palestinian communities among Gaza’s ruins.

The Israel Defense Forces deny targeting farmers or any civilians, saying they have only responded to imminent threats from Hamas since the October ceasefire.

Despite the risks, Abu Rabee, 48, is still at work every day cultivating a 1.4-hectare (3.4-acre) plot in Beit Lahiya that was an orchard of orange trees before the war. He said the orchard was bulldozed by the Israeli army.

“We cleared it and rehabilitated it using only basic tools, manual labour and tremendous human effort. It took a great deal of time and hard work before it was ready for cultivation again,” he said.

Out of that scrap of land, Abu Rabee says his family have produced hundreds of thousands of aubergine, tomato and pepper seedlings. They raise cash by growing their own aubergines to sell to wholesale traders, while most of the seedlings are distributed to other farmers or to individual households to plant in patches of earth around their homes and tents.

He says the supply has transformed the local food market. Aubergines now cost less than two shekels a kilogram, compared with 40 shekels a few months ago. Peppers and mulukhiyah, a dark green leafy vegetable, are now selling at a tenth of their market price earlier this year.
sources.headline: On scraps of land and under constant threat, Gaza farmers struggle to survive

stories.headline: Norway mourns King Harald V as Crown Prince Haakon prepares to succeed him

sources.body:
Norwegians gather to remember monarch whose death comes amid scandal over links between crown princess and Jeffrey Epstein

Norwegians have gathered in their thousands to pay their respects to King Harald V, Europe’s oldest reigning monarch, who has died, aged 89, in Oslo. He was succeeded immediately by his son, King Haakon VIII.

The new king thanked “the government and Norwegian people for their support and sympathy for the royal family at this time”. A period of national mourning was announced as crowds left wreaths and messages outside the royal palace in Oslo.

Flags around the country were lowered to half mast and church bells rang out at midday. “An era has ended. A new one begins. The king is dead. Long live the king,” the prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, said after meeting Haakon.

The new king, whose wife, Mette-Marit, has recently come under scrutiny over scandals including a much-criticised association with the late US child sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, formally notified the government of his father’s death on Friday morning.

Haakon, 53, told the cabinet at an extraordinary council of state that he would take the name Haakon VIII, as expected. He also chose as his personal motto: “Everything for Norway .”

The new king will swear an oath of accession in parliament within the next few days. Coronation ceremonies were abolished in Norway more than a century ago, but Haakon could choose to have his reign blessed at a consecration ceremony.

The palace had said on Thursday that Harald’s health had deteriorated and that the king, who was seen as a unifying figure and a force for stability amid a string of recent family scandals, was in an “extremely serious” condition.

Støre said earlier that he had received the news “with deep sadness”, adding: “A whole nation is in mourning, and ⁠the people of Norway are left with a ​deep sense of ‌gratitude for a ‌long life in the service of Norway.”

Royalty around Europe sent their condolences, with Spain’s royal family hailing Harald’s “responsibility, dignity, humility and tireless dedication”, and Denmark’s King Frederik and Queen Mary saying he was “loved like few others”.

King Carl XVI Gustaf, of Sweden, said: “Throughout the years, King Harald has been a good friend to me, my family, and to Sweden … I ​wish ​my dear godson Haakon, ​who now succeeds his father as head ​of state, ‌success and ​good ​fortune.”

Belgium’s royal family recalled Harald’s “humour, humanity and sincerity”, while Britain’s King Charles mourned the loss of his “dear cousin”, paying tribute to a “towering figure” who guided his country with “warmth and humility”.

Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, said Norway had “lost a great figure who stood for prudence and unity”, and the French president, Emmanuel Macron, expressed “deep sadness”.

Norway’s ceremonial head of state since 1991, Harald was being treated in Oslo’s University hospital for haemolytic anaemia, a condition caused by an abnormally rapid destruction of the body’s red blood cells.
sources.headline: Norway’s King Harald dies aged 89

sources.body: Norway is mourning King Harald V after the country's longest-serving monarch died at the age of 89, with tributes pouring in from across Europe. His death paves the way for Crown Prince Haakon to become king, as the royal family faces renewed scrutiny over Crown Princess Mette-Marit's reported past ties to Jeffrey Epstein and the conviction of her son for rape.
sources.headline: Norway mourns King Harald as Haakon prepares to take the throne

stories.headline: Russia is losing thousands more troops each month than it can recruit, Western officials say

sources.body:
Moscow recruits an estimated 1,000 people a day, but officials say it cannot keep up with its level of casualties

Russia is losing about 6,000 more troops in Ukraine each month than it can recruit, western officials have said.

While Russia is still acquiring new battlefield recruits at speed, with an estimated rate of 1,000 a day, in the last two months even this has not been sufficient to replace those killed or injured.

“We estimate that the gap between the number of people Russia is losing to casualties and the number they’re being able to recruit is around 6,000 a month at the moment,” one western official said.

“Putin’s response to this has been to escalate himself and to target civilian infrastructure and civilians in Ukraine, firing over 360 missiles since early July and exploiting Kyiv’s shortage of defence against ballistic missiles. It’s clear that Moscow intends to try and break Ukrainian morale by destroying its energy infrastructure this winter.”

Such tactics are in part because Putin has limited options for overcoming the huge losses on the battlefield with more recruitment.

Western officials believe further mobilisation would be a big risk both politically and economically, saying the last such event, in autumn 2022 , saw about a million, often highly skilled, Russians leave the country, with less than half returning.

It is also unclear whether the Russia military could absorb the several hundred thousand new recruits which would result, given a lack of equipment and officers.

Ukraine has repeatedly attacked Russian targets connected to oil, creating fuel shortages, but has appealed repeatedly for more help from allies, both with offensive missiles and defence systems.

Andy Burnham visited Kyiv on his first overseas trip as prime minister this week. He told Volodymyr Zelenskyy that the UK would give Ukraine previously classified information on the British-manufactured components for long-range cruise missiles.

Burnham has also urged the international community to do more to protect Ukraine against Russian attacks, particularly with more US-made Patriot interceptor missiles. He is expected to make this argument at next month’s UN general assembly in New York.

In response, Russia has made repeated threats of retaliation, including talk of attacks on UK military targets both inside and outside Ukraine.

The western officials said that while the threat from Russia remained very real, the situation had not changed, and the assessment was that “Putin absolutely wants to avoid a direct confrontation with Nato”.

One official said: “We are seeing a continuation of hostile rhetoric and various accusations against the UK. This is absolutely consistent with longstanding Russian military doctrine, which is to use rhetoric to both exploit fears in adversaries and to influence decision-making. So this is not a new phenomenon.”

Officials say Russia still has the capability to target the UK, with cyberattacks or physical attacks on civilian targets by proxies, for example factories or warehouses.
sources.headline: Russia losing 6,000 more troops than it can recruit each month in Ukraine, says west

After repeated disappointments over US Patriots, Ukraine switches to attacking Russian ballistic production using European weapons.

Ukraine has reinforced the defence of its eastern Donetsk region as Russia mounted renewed efforts to seize Sloviansk, a key part of Ukraine’s “fortress belt” of cities that include Kramatorsk, Druzhkivka and Kostiantynivka.

At the same time, Britain and France made a crucial decision to transfer Storm Shadow cruise missile technology to Kyiv, as Ukraine shifts its air defence strategy to destroying Russia’s means of ballistic missile production and launch, rather than intercepting the missiles individually.

Ukrainian commander-in-chief Mykhailo Drapatyi made the first major decision of his new command on August 26 to reinforce two units defending Sloviansk.

Russia has also been infiltrating the fortress city of Kostiantynivka to the south of Sloviansk, but does not control it.

Ukrainian military observer Kostyantyn Mashovets said Kyiv still maintains positions in central and northern Kostiantynivka.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said 70-80 percent of Russian casualties were taking place on the Kostiantynivka front. He estimated Russian losses this year at 267,000, including at least 155,000 killed.

Russian commander-in-chief Valery Gerasimov said on Thursday that his troops were within four kilometres (2.5 miles) of Sloviansk.

But maps published by Deep State and the Institute for the Study of War, which observe territorial changes through geo-located, open-source information, suggest Russian troops are between 12km (7.4 miles) and 16km (10 miles) of Sloviansk.

Ukraine is pressing a campaign to hobble the supply of Russian men, munitions and fuel to the front line by targeting storages, airfields and transport routes.

It has been largely successful in bringing Russia to a standstill.

The ISW estimated Russia has lost 27 square kilometres (10.4 square miles) in August, and at least 233sq km (90sq miles) this year.

On August 20, Ukraine destroyed 18 buildings storing aerial drones at the Primorsko-Akhtarsk airfield in Krasnodar Krai, just across the Sea of Azov from Crimea, and a Sukhoi-24 fighter at the Saky airfield in Crimea itself.

Two days later, Ukraine’s unmanned systems destroyed a Sukhoi-33 fighter and a MiG-29 fighter at the Vityazevo airfield in Krasnodar, along with a strike and reconnaissance Orion drone. On the same day, they struck an oil trans-shipment terminal at Yeisk, in Krasnodar.

On August 24, Ukraine destroyed another MiG-29 at Millerovo airfield in Rostov.

Ukraine also targeted and destroyed ballistic missile launchers and radar complexes.

It has hit a dozen Russian military supply vessels, bringing the total number of ships disabled during the campaign to 242.

Separately, Ukraine has struck 267 Crimean power stations and substations in six weeks. The result has been a near-blackout across the Crimean Peninsula.

Russia-installed head of Crimea Sergey Aksyonov acknowledged “objective difficulties that cannot be resolved in the short term for technical reasons”.
sources.headline: Ukraine reinforces Donetsk as it seeks to disrupt Russia’s weapons flow

stories.headline: Meta reaches major settlement with US states over alleged harms to young users

sources.body:
Other governments could seek similar concessions, while separate legal action is pending in places ranging from Kenya to the Netherlands

I n October 2021, Abrham Meareg’s father, a professor of chemistry in Ethiopia’s northern town of Bahir Dar, was shot at close range and died outside his family home. This was in the middle of the country’s civil war.

For weeks, Facebook’s algorithm had actively promoted posts calling for the academic to be murdered, according to Meareg and Foxglove, a nonprofit organisation supporting Meareg’s lawsuit against the company in Kenya. These posts included photos of his father and his home address.

Meareg filed the lawsuit in 2022. He said he repeatedly asked Facebook to remove the posts and the company did nothing. Nearly four years later, the case has still not been heard. Foxglove said Meta, Facebook’s parent company, had “fought tooth and nail to avoid responsibility”.

Meareg said: “It’s a matter of numbers to them, a matter of statistics. It has been proven multiple times that our lives do not matter to them.”

On Wednesday, Meta settled a lawsuit brought by 29 US states who argued it had designed addictive products that hooked young people. The social media company agreed to pay $18bn and to change certain features of its platform in the US. California’s attorney general said it was a victory that would make “a world of difference for children and their families”.

But elsewhere in the world, in jurisdictions as far flung as Amsterdam and Nairobi, other claims have yet to be heard. Far bigger questions about the power of a single US technology company to shape politics and democracy everywhere on Earth are still to be answered.

For the US, the settlement is a victory. A jury has done what the US Congress could not – put controls on a powerful tech company. As a part of the settlement, Meta has said it will set time limits on children’s use of its platforms Facebook and Instagram and block night-time usage.

For Meta, the settlement is also a victory. Its share price rose in the hours after the deal was announced. Its CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, was not forced to testify. The sum it is to pay, while not meaningless, is far less than the states had sought – $200bn – or the amount Meta itself had suggested in a court filing it might have to pay, which was up to $1.4tn.

For the rest of the world, however, the picture is more mixed. The limits Meta will put on its US platform are, in large part, similar to limits the UK and Australia have already achieved through regulation. There are certain concessions Meta has now made that other governments could also demand: for example, while the UK plans to ban under-16s from social media platforms, it may wish to ask Meta to impose a default daily use limit of two hours for under-18s, which is what the company has agreed to in the US.

None of this meaningfully changes the equation for Meareg or what his case represents, which is that a massive US company, unaccountable to voters, unbound by transparency requirements, owns a worldwide digital commons that shapes reality for billions of people.
sources.headline: What could Meta’s US settlement mean around the world – and what now for other claims against firm?

Meta pagarà fins a 17.000 milions de dòlars per estalviar-se el judici per l'addicció dels menors a les seves xarxes socials, Facebook i Instagram . Malgrat aquesta xifra econòmica elevada, alguns analistes consideren que no s'ha fet prou i que l'empresa en surt molt ben parada.

Experts com Josep Maria Ganyet , enginyer informàtic i professor de Comunicació Audiovisual de la Universitat Pompeu Fabra, ha explicat en una entrevista a 3CatInfo que hi havia en joc prendre mesures "molt dràstiques per evitar que les xarxes fomentin l'addicció". Unes mesures que, amb l'acord d'aquest dimecres, finalment "queden molt curtes" , diu.

Segons Ganyet, amb aquest pacte Meta ha aconseguit no haver de tocar alguns dels aspectes més addictius de les plataformes, com les stories que desapareixen en 24 hores i l'scroll infinit . En canvi, "sí que s'ha avingut a controlar el temps que els més joves passen" a les xarxes.

Sobre les stories i l'scroll infinit, Ganyet alerta que Meta fa servir tècniques similars a les que s'utilitzen als casinos perquè els usuaris "perdin la noció del temps". I planteja que si els menors no poden entrar en aquests establiments, també haurien de tenir més restringit l'accés a les plataformes digitals.

Ens hem quedat a mig camí. Havíem d'anar mes enllà, al moll de l'os.

Si bé és cert que no posa fi a l'scroll infinit, Meta es compromet a introduir dos canvis per posar-hi fre. D'una banda, els comptes dels menors ja no reproduiran per defecte un vídeo darrere l'altre, sinó que caldrà que facin un gest –lliscar, per exemple– per passar al contingut següent. I, de l'altra, cada 15 minuts de reproducció de vídeos les plataformes faran una pausa .

De fet, a casa nostra, la Comissió Europea investiga si l'scroll infinit va en contra de les lleis europees , i podria acabar obligant Meta a aplicar restriccions similars a les que s'ha compromès als Estats Units.

Així ho assegura Toni Noguera , periodista especialitzat en tecnologia de 3CatInfo . Noguera també exposa que l'acord de Meta "no ens afectarà directament", als europeus, però el fet que hagin d'aplicar canvis en el desenvolupament de les seves plataformes als Estats Units indica que aquestes novetats ens acabaran arribant també a nosaltres.

Noguera reflexiona sobre el fet que Meta no entri al detall del contingut que mostren les plataformes, ni de restringir els temes que hi surten, sinó de "com es dissenyen les aplicacions" . Ha quedat demostrat que la companyia guanya diners "a costa de la salut mental de persones vulnerables", i també que "coneixien els efectes perniciosos" de les seves apps i, tot i això, han seguit distribuint els seus productes.

Que la jugada li ha sortit prou bé a Meta ho demostra també que la seva cotització a la borsa no se n'ha ressentit. Les accions van tancar aquest dimecres amb un creixement de l'1% , i en alguns moments del dia van estar per sobre del 4%.

Després de conèixer les novetats judicials de la companyia als Estats Units, aquest dijous s'ha pronunciat la Comissió Europea .
sources.headline: Claus de la multa multimilionària a Meta: limitacions i com afecta Europa

stories.headline: Trump signs order renaming Lake Ontario “Lake America,” escalating tensions with Canada

President Donald Trump says he’s renaming Lake Ontario to “Lake America” in the United States as he exacerbates his trade war with Canada. Trump signed an executive order Thursday that updated the lake’s name for the U.S. geographic naming service.

sources.body:
Mark Carney rejects attempt to rename lake as did several US governors, with Tony Evers mocking the move

Donald Trump signed an executive order on Thursday directing the federal government to rename Lake Ontario, making it Lake America, amid his escalating trade war with Canada.

The order directs federal agencies to adopt the name-change on US maps, documents and databases. But Trump has no authority to rename Canada’s portion of the lake, nor to compel Canada , international legal bodies, international mapmakers or the rest of the world to adopt a new name.

The move follows a similar action the president took on the first day of his second term in office, when he signed an order renaming the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America”.

“We have a gulf and we have a lake – now all we need is an ocean. Maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific,” he told reporters, sitting at the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office. “Maybe we’ll change them both.”

Propped behind the US president was a large map of the Great Lakes region, with “Lake America” printed in red lettering above Lake Ontario.

Mark Carney, Canada’s prime minister, rejected the US’s attempt to rename the body of water, explaining in a post on social media that its name comes from the language of the Indigenous Wendat people and predates both the Canadian Confederation and the US Declaration of Independence.

“We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms,” he wrote on X. “Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always.”

Tim Houston, the premier of Nova Scotia, responded: “We’re into some real foolishness now. It’s Lake Ontario, buddy.”

Several US governors in the Great Lakes region also dismissed the name change.

“New York won’t be calling it that,” the state’s governor, Democrat Kathy Hochul replied . New York borders the lake.

Michigan’s governor, Gretchen Whitmer, a Democrat, recalled that schoolchildren learn the acronym H-O-M-E-S for the names of the five great lakes: Huron, Ontario, Michigan, Erie, Superior. And the Wisconsin governor, Democrat Tony Evers, mocked the move by sharing a video of himself changing the name of Lake Michigan to Lake Wisconsin, signed on a restaurant napkin.

The latest tweak of Canada’s nose by the US president comes as tensions increase between the US and its northern neighbor. Over the weekend, trade talks between Washington and Ottawa collapsed and the US imposed a 50% tariff on several Canadian imports, with Trump threatening another round of 50% duties on Canadian steel, trucks, cars and auto parts to take effect in the new year. Carney hit back with 25-50% tariffs on hundreds of US goods.

“They want to be treated like a state, but they’re not a state,” Trump said, a nod to his previous suggestions that Canada should become the “51st state” in the union, a prospect that has enraged Canadians. “But they want to be treated like they’re a state, and so we just can’t do that any more.”

An inspection contractor found a chemical tank at a Washington state paper mill “not fit for continued service” 10 months before it failed in May, killing 11 in one of the deadliest U.S. workplace disasters in recent decades, according to a federal report released Friday.

The U.S. Chemical Safety Board’s update about the May 26 failure in Longview, which expelled enough caustic liquid to blow out building walls, is part of an ongoing investigation. The federal agency said it is still determining the cause of the failure.

The board found that the contractor provided Nippon Dynawave Packaging Company with recommendations for internal inspections and shell repairs, but the company did none between a July 2025 inspection and the May 2026 failure.

“Because the investigation remains ongoing, we will not comment on individual findings or documents at this time,” an emailed statement from Nippon spokesperson Sam Jefferies said Friday. “Our focus remains on supporting affected families and employees and taking the necessary steps toward fully reopening the Longview facility.”

Jefferies said the company will continue to cooperate fully with the board.

The Association of Western Pulp and Paper Workers released a statement on Friday saying the board’s findings were “deeply troubling.”

“The update raises urgent questions about how technical findings and recommendations concerning the tank were communicated, evaluated and incorporated into decisions about its continued operation,” the statement said. “The families and workforce deserve a complete accounting of that process.”

A lawyer representing the family of two brothers who were killed, Tyler and Bradley Covington, said the board’s findings are “nothing short of alarming.”

“When safety inspections and recommendations don’t lead to action, danger becomes a reality that causes devastation to human life,” lawyer Kyle Findley said in a statement Friday. “We will continue to work tirelessly to ensure those responsible for this horrific accident are held accountable and their families receive justice.”

Federal immigration authorities have detained dozens of people in the city of Danbury, Connecticut, this week, despite intense opposition from elected officials and protesters.

The Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign is plowing ahead even in Democratic-led states like Connecticut that have laws seeking to limit Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s power. Nationwide, ICE arrests increased significantly in June and July, according to newly released data.

ICE officers, some wearing masks, have detained people outside Danbury apartment buildings, during traffic stops, in parks, near an elementary school, and outside a daycare center, according to the mayor and local activists tracking the operation that began Monday.

Agents detained one father who walked his child to a bus stop shortly after the school bus drove off, said Clementina Lunar, an advocate with the group Danbury Unites for Immigrants. Her group said that, as of Wednesday evening, more than 50 arrests had ripped apart 40 families, and many others were hiding in fear.

“We are talking about mothers with babies and school-age children who unfortunately had their breadwinner taken,” Lunar said. “ICE has been terrorizing” the city, she added.

Nearly one-third of the city’s 90,000 people are Hispanic or Latino, according to the U.S. Census Bureau, and slightly more were born in another country.

The Department of Homeland Security said its ICE agents had addressed several “public safety threats,” arresting at least four people convicted of violent crimes after entering the U.S. illegally.

Local, state and federal representatives from Connecticut held a news conference Wednesday to denounce ICE’s operation, which they said was traumatizing some young students just as they are returning to public schools.

sources.body: <p>La situación social se desborda por momentos en Ceuta. Pero al menos habían logrado algo sin problemas: alimentarlos cada día, para evitar conflictos mayores, asaltos a supermercados o cualquier tumulto similar que se produce cuando un grupo grande de personas pasa hambre y tiene comida cerca. Ahora, incluso eso se ha convertido en un problema serio, porque en los últimos dos días, un grupo cada vez mayor de ciudadanos <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-08-27/crece-la-tension-en-una-ceuta-al-borde-del-estallido-social.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-08-27/crece-la-tension-en-una-ceuta-al-borde-del-estallido-social.html">intenta impedir el reparto de comida diario en la playa de El Trampolín</a>. El ministro del Interior, Fernando Grande- Marlaska, ha reiterado este viernes que de los informes previos no se podía "referir de repente", ni nadie pudo "prever" una entrada masiva de inmigrantes en Ceuta como la que hubo los días 30 y 31 de julio .

"Hasta el 29 de julio se produjeron 1.026 entradas a nado y se realizaron 2.857 interceptaciones por parte de Marruecos. (...). Durante julio y hasta el 30 fue un incremento diario pero las interceptaciones marroquíes eran muy superiores y no era preocupante. Querer decir o referir que de repente hay una razón para sospechar que de 300 en un día, o máximo 400, pasemos a 72.000, me parece que no puede realizarse ", ha subrayado en la Comisión de Interior del Congreso donde ha comparecido a petición propia para explicar la actuación de su departamento en la crisis.

En este sentido, ha resaltado que "lo que se hablaba en esos informes" previos a la llegada masiva de inmigrantes era "como otros años". " Que no digan que lo del 30 alguien lo veía o lo decía porque no es cierto ", ha zanjado.

Así, ha vuelto a contradecir, como hiciera también el pasado martes en rueda de prensa tras el Consejo de Ministros, a la ministra de Defensa, Margarita Robles , que, en la comisión del ramo en el Congreso el pasado martes, aseguró que el Centro Nacional de Inteligencia (CNI) avisó el día previo de la entrada a nado de inmigrantes.

En el mismo sentido que Marlaska, este jueves se pronunció el ministro de Presidencia, Justicia y Relaciones con las Cortes, Félix Bolaños , quien defendió en la comisión mixta de Seguridad Nacional que no hubo "información previa, ni precisa" de que fueran a entrar miles de personas en Ceuta.

En su primera intervención en la comisión, Marlaska ha evitado pronunciarse sobre este polémica, pero tras las reiteradas preguntas de los grupos parlamentarios en sus turnos de réplica, el ministro ha admitido que lo único que se sabía antes del 30 y 31 de julio es que se estaban produciendo entradas a nado durante el mes de julio , pero que eran cifras similares a veranos anteriores.

"¿Si alguien lo hubiera visto, con el recuerdo que teníamos de mayo de 2021 - cuando entraron en Ceuta 10.000 inmigrantes -, no se habría elevado en la forma que todos podemos entender?", ha cuestionado de manera retórica.

Según Marlaska, las causas de la entrada de miles de migrantes en Ceuta fueron "plurales" . Asimismo ha descargado de culpa al CNI, al Centro de Inteligencia de las Fuerzas Armadas (CIFAS), a los servicios de información de la Policía Nacional, la Guardia Civil e incluso el servicio exterior de la Unión Europea.

"Los servicios de información del Estado siempre funcionan. Yo no he responsabilizado nunca a ningún servicio de información, sean CNI, CIFAS, Policía Nacional o Guardia Civil", ha sostenido Marlaska en el turno de réplica a los grupos.

El ministro ha asegurado que entre esas causas "purales" están los " bulos en las redes sociales, la utilización indebida de la interpretación de una sentencia -la del Tribunal Supremo que impedía las devoluciones en caliente si los inmigrantes llegan por mar -, o desinformaciones sobre el estado y seguridad de la frontera".

La chispa que sitúa a Ceuta al borde del estallido social comenzó ayer a prender. Literalmente. Tras días en los que la crispación empezaba a desbordar la ciudad autónoma, la playa de Benítez se convirtió en la estampa que retrata el estado de la ciudad autónoma casi un mes después de la entrada masiva de más de 80.000 personas. Un cordón de antidisturbios separa dos realidades: delante de los policías centenares de ceutíes cada vez más hartos claman por la inmediata expulsión de los “invasores”; detrás de los agentes, también centenares de inmigrantes, desafiantes, muestran su intención de resistir, de no volver a su país. El humo, como de una olla a presión a punto de saltar por los aires, envuelve la playa. La humareda sale de las chozas del campamento que un grupo de vecinos han prendido, después de arrasarlo. Ni unos ni otros dan ya su brazo a torcer. Los manifestantes se van, la Policía se despliega, los magrebíes vuelven a levantar el asentamiento.

La llamada a la calma del Gobierno central, a través del mando único en la crisis, Ángel Víctor Torres, cayó en saco rato. El ministro de Política Territorial fue sincero: “No puedo prometer devoluciones mañana”. Y es ahí donde está el fondo de la cuestión. Los ceutíes entienden que tras semanas con promesas que no se materializan no hay otro camino que “la expulsión de todos” los que llegaron irregularmente desde Marruecos. El mismo objetivo que persigue el Ejecutivo -con la salvedad de los menores de edad y los asilados-, pero el tiempo que se dan los ceutíes y el que maneja Moncloa no coincide. La paciencia a los primeros se les ha agotado. De ahí que el episodio de la quema de parte del campamento de inmigrantes fuese, por ahora, el último de la espiral de violencia en la que ha derivado el enfado de los caballas.

Tras una madrugada en la que se registraron cacerías de inmigrantes a manos de ultras, un grupo de marroquíes tendieron una emboscada planificada a un vehículo militar, cuya parte delantera terminó destrozada. Según fuentes policiales, en torno a las 5:30 horas entre 30 y 40 personas que se encontraban agazapadas alrededor del puesto de vigilancia establecido en el barrio de Bezú rodearon al transporte de las fuerzas armadas con palos y piedras de grandes dimensiones. La violencia de los agresores provocó la huida a píe de los cuatro militares del Grupo de Regulares número 54 que iban en el vehículo. Mientras trataban de ponerse a salvo, según las mismas fuentes, recibieron pedradas, que les provocaron heridas leves por las que tuvieron que ser atendidos. La Policía Nacional que salió en auxilio de los uniformados logró detener a 12 de los presuntos agresores. Las imágenes del vehículo con las lunas rotas corrieron como la pólvora entre grupos de vecinos en WhatsApp, provocando una gran indignación.

Como también se viralizó la convocatoria para impedir que se repartan más alimentos entre inmigrantes en la Playa del Trampolín. Un centenar de vecinos acudieron a la llamada, realizando una sentada en la mitad de la avenida que provocó que el convoy de la Cruz Roja se tuviese que dar la vuelta. Con el lema por bandera “Ceuta no se vende, Ceuta se defiende”, los manifestantes consideraban que “si se sigue alimentando” a las personas que entraron irregularmente “nunca volverán a su país”. Expulsión inmediata o asfixia. Finalmente, la comida (y el agua) pudo ser repartida, como cada tarde, gracias a otro fuerte despliegue policial en los accesos al Trampolín. Y cuando todas las miradas estaban puestas en los vehículos de Cruz Roja, llegó el asalto a la Playa de Benítez, donde las chozas quedaron reducidas a cenizas.
sources.headline: La tensión entre los vecinos y los migrantes se dispara en Ceuta

stories.headline: Spain’s inflation rises above 4% in August, driven by fuel prices

sources.body:
La persistente subida de los precios del petróleo por el conflicto de Irán y el cierre del estrecho de Ormuz impacta ya con intensidad en los precios. La inflación general repunta en agosto, situándose en el 4,3%, según los indicador adelantado del IPC del Instituto Nacional de Estadística, siete décimas por encima de la registrada en julio y la tasa más alta de los últimos tres años, desde febrero de 2023. Con el dato de agosto, la inflación encadena dos meses consecutivos de ascensos y se sitúa por encima del 4% por primera vez desde abril de 2023.

En este comportamiento, explica el INE, influyen los precios de los combustibles y lubricantes para vehículos personales, que suben mientras que en agosto de 2025 bajaron; y también, aunque en menor medida, los alimentos y bebidas no alcohólicas, cuyos precios descienden menos que en el mismo mes del año pasado.

El repunte de la inflación general no se traslada de momento a la inflación subyacente, que excluye de su cálculo energía y alimentos no elaborados. Esta tasa desciende una décima en agosto, hasta el 2,9% interanual.

Tras tres meses consecutivos, desde marzo, con la inflación manteniéndose en el 3,2%, en julio, el IPC repuntó tres décimas hasta situarse en el 3,5%.

El ministerio de Economía, Comercio y Empresa recordó, al publicarse estos datos, que las medidas del Plan de Respuesta siguen vigentes según el calendario ya anunciado: la rebaja del Impuesto sobre Hidrocarburos aplicable al gasóleo se eleva a 20 céntimos por litro desde el 1 de septiembre, mientras que la rebaja de la gasolina se mantiene en 5 céntimos por litro. El resto de las medidas continúa activo según lo previsto en el Real Decreto-ley 18/2026.

“El Gobierno mantiene un seguimiento minuto a minuto del impacto del conflicto en Irán sobre la economía española, de la mano de los agentes sociales y los sectores más afectados”, afirmaron.

En términos mensuales (agosto sobre julio), el IPC subió un 0,7%, cuatro décimas más que en julio y su mayor avance mensual desde el pasado mes de marzo. Atendiendo sólo a los meses de agosto, la subida de este mes es la más elevada en un mes de agosto desde el año 1992.

Con el incremento registrado en el octavo mes del año, la inflación mensual acumula siete meses consecutivos de alzas.

Por su parte, el IPC armonizado (IPCA) incremento seis décimas su tasa interanual en agosto, hasta el 4,5%, con una variación mensual del 0,6%. La inflación subyacente del IPCA se estima en un 3,2% para el octavo mes del año, según apunta Estadística.

El detalle del IPC de julio publicado por el INE a mediados de este mes confirmó que la subclase del gasóleo registró una variación interanual del 15,7% en julio, por encima del umbral del 15% previsto en el decreto de medidas para contener el impacto de la guerra en Irán.

Al superarse ese umbral, se activa de forma automática la cláusula de salvaguarda del Plan de Respuesta del Gobierno al conflicto en Oriente Próximo. La rebaja del Impuesto sobre Hidrocarburos aplicable al gasóleo se elevará a 20 céntimos por litro el próximo 1 de septiembre, frente a los 5 céntimos inicialmente previstos para ese mes.

Els preus s'han disparat a l'agost més del que es preveia. La inflació al conjunt de l'Estat ha pujat 7 dècimes aquest mes d'agost i situa la taxa interanual de l'IPC avançat en el 4,3%. Una xifra que, si es confirma, serà la més alta en més de 3 anys.

L'Institut Nacional d'Estadística (INE) atribueix aquest fort repunt a l'encariment dels combustibles i, en menor mesura, a l'evolució del preu dels aliments i les begudes no alcohòliques .

Amb aquesta pujada, la inflació encadena dos mesos consecutius d'ascensos i se situa en el nivell més alt des de febrer de 2023 , quan en plena crisi energètica per la guerra d'Ucraïna va escalar fins al 6% .

Des del Ministeri d'Economia assenyalen que "la inflació general a l'agost se situa al 4,3% en el càlcul interanual, degut principalment a l'encariment dels carburants per la persistència del xoc energètic derivat de la guerra a l'Iran".

Precisament l' encariment del gasoil ja el mes passat va activar un increment de les ajudes , que entraran en vigor aquest setembre. A partir de dimarts que ve, la rebaixa de l'impost sobre hidrocarburs serà de 20 cèntims per litre ; en la gasolina es mantindran els 5 cèntims previstos.

El principal culpable de la pujada de preus de l'agost és el gas , que amb les tensions per la guerra a l'Iran i l'increment de la demanda no només ha encarit els carburants. També es notarà a la factura de la llum, que per si sola ja hagués pujat per l'ús de l'aire condicionat en un estiu especialment calorós.

La calor extrema ha fet que hagi pujat la necessitat de climatitzar les cases especialment al vespre, just quan cau la producció fotovoltaica .

És llavors quan el sistema ha de recórrer a altres tecnologies. I aquí tornem a topar amb el gas, com explica Maria Llop, catedràtica d'Economia de la Universitat Rovira i Virgili .

Quan hi ha pics de demanda i s'ha de recórrer a cicles combinats, que utilitzen gas, és el preu del gas i el cost de fabricació de l'electricitat els que en determinen el preu final.

Tot plegat tindrà un impacte a la factura de la llum que no serà igual per a tothom .

Els usuaris del mercat lliure ho notaran quan els revisin els contractes, mentre que els del mercat regulat ja ho estan patint ara.

Per l'organització de consumidors FACUA es tracta d'un bé de primera necessitat que el govern espanyol hauria de garantir intervenint en el mercat .

Ja sigui a través d'impostos o de topalls en el preu de l'energia per tal que les famílies tinguin un preu estable

FACUA calcula que el rebut d'un usuari mitjà superarà aquest agost els 100 euros . La primera vegada que això passa en 4 anys. És un 20% més de factura que fa un any i un 10% més que al juliol.

Aquesta situació registrada a l'agost també torna a posar sobre la taula un dels reptes del nou sistema energètic: aprofitar l'excedent solar del migdia i emmagatzemar-lo per poder-lo utilitzar quan cau el sol i la demanda encara és alta. Una solució que, a priori, ajudaria a contenir els preus.

Mentre l'indicador general s'ha disparat, la inflació subjacent –sense aliments no elaborats ni productes energètics, que són els elements més volàtils– ha baixat una dècima respecte del mes passat i s'ha situat en el 2,9% interanual.

stories.headline: Families displaced by the Putxet metro-work sinkhole may not return home until early 2027

sources.body:
Divuit famílies del barri de Sant Gervasi-la Bonanova desallotjades al juliol per l'enfonsament parcial d'un interior d'illa a causa de les obres de l'L9 del metro no podran tornar a casa fins al gener de l'any vinent.

Tampoc podran reobrir aquest any set dels vuit comerços del barri del Putxet, a Barcelona, que encara estan tancats per aquell ensorrament. Ho ha anunciat aquest divendres la delegada del govern de la Generalitat a Barcelona, Pilar Díaz , després de reunir-se amb els veïns i comerciants afectats.

Díaz ha explicat que, dels 87 habitatges i setze comerços afectats inicialment, de vuit finques dels carrers Rubinstein i Teodora Lamadrid, fins ara ja s'ha autoritzat el retorn a casa de 54 famílies de quatre finques i la reobertura de vuit comerços. El retorn d'aquests veïns era "voluntari" , segons va explicar aquest agost l'alcalde de Barcelona, Jaume Collboni.

L'esvoranc, de vuit metres de diàmetre i quatre metres de profunditat , es va localitzar a l' interior del restaurant pizzeria Verona . I va afectar un pati interior i un petit magatzem.

Però encara hi ha 33 veïns i vuit locals comercials pendents de poder tornar a la normalitat. D'aquests, es preveu que quinze famílies i un local comercial puguin tornar d'aquí cinc o sis setmanes, és a dir, a finals de setembre o principis d'octubre . Però la resta no podran fer-ho a curt termini.

Els veïns que no podran tornar, de moment, són els de les finques dels carrers Rubinstein, 2 i 4, i de Teodora Lamadrid, 3 , "per seguretat, per finalitzar les feines de consolidació del terreny i posar la tuneladora en marxa", segons ha explicat Pilar Díaz.

Díaz ha dit que això és el que marquen els protocols, "que han estat millorats" després d'aquest incident. I ha assegurat que es reforçaran les oficines d'atenció als veïns i comerços afectats. Pilar Díaz també ha dit que s'està treballant en la millora i simplificació dels tràmits per cobrar "les bestretes, avançaments econòmics i ajuts " que puguin necessitar tots els afectats.

El director general d'Infraestructures i Mobilitat del Departament de Territori de la Generalitat, Ramon Ramírez , ha explicat que el retard en el retorn d'aquestes famílies i comerços es deu a les feines de consolidació del terreny que encara s'han de fer. I que no depenen dels recursos que s'hi aboquin, sinó "de la quantitat de material que el terreny accepta".

També ha assegurat que no té res a veure amb l'esquerda que es va detectar fa un mes, la nit del 29 al 30 de juliol, a la finca del carrer Rubinstein, 2, i que ja es va resoldre, ha dit, "amb el reforç de l'edifici".

Ramon Ramírez ha explicat que, després de moltes hores d'injecció de ciment, ja poden fer una estimació del temps que els portarà consolidar el terreny i treure al carrer la màquina que hi ha a sota d'aquests edificis . Uns treballs que no es podran acabar, almenys, fins a finals d'aquest any.

A Rubinstein 2, l'única finca que va patir danys estructurals, encara hi ha "danys més importants que requereixen un procés de reparació més llarg", ha reconegut. Ramírez creu que "a començaments de l'any vinent podrem parlar del retorn de les famílies dels divuit habitatges i set comerços" encara pendents.
sources.headline: Divuit famílies afectades per l'esvoranc de l'L9 no podran tornar a casa fins al gener del 2027

sources.body:
Más de un tercio de vecinos afectados por el socavón ocasionado por las obras de la L9 del metro en el barrio del Putxet el pasado 7 de julio llevan todo el verano sin poder volver a sus casas. La última noticia que recibieron, antes de que empezara agosto, fue que una nueva grieta encontrada en el subterráneo del número 2 de la calle Rubinstein retrasaría hasta al menos este septiembre su retorno. Este viernes, Pilar Díaz, delegada del Govern en Barcelona, ha anunciado que una de las cuatro fincas que quedaban por volver podrá hacerlo en unas cinco o seis semanas, pero el resto deberá esperar hasta principios de 2027 .

Así lo ha explicado este viernes en declaraciones a medios junto a Ramón Ramírez , Director General d'Infraestructures de Mobilitat de la Generalitat, y Sebastià Massagué , director de Bombers de Barcelona, quienes han desvinculado la nueva grieta hallada a finales de julio con el retraso del regreso de los vecinos. En concreto, tienen luz verde para volver entre finales de septiembre y principios de octubre 15 viviendas y un local ubicados en el bloque 5 de la calle Teodora Lamadrid , mientras que los números 2 y 4 de la calle Rubinstein y el 3 de Teodora Lamadrid no tendrán más noticias hasta las puertas del año que viene.

"Se tienen que hacer todas las tareas de consolidación del terreno , y eso no depende estrictamente de los recursos que pongamos sino de la cantidad de material que el terreno acepta", ha argumentado Ramírez, quien ha especificado que hasta principios de año no se podrá establecer una fecha de retorno concreta para los afectados.

De hecho, durante este verano se han realizado todo tipo de trabajos para garantizar la solidez del terreno , con sistemas de excultación e inspección para que los desperfectos se reparasen lo antes posible. Sin embargo, el departamento no tomará una decisión apresurada sin antes el visto bueno de los técnicos. Durante este periodo, "los trabajos han avanzado con buen ritmo " y la situación se mantiene "estable " desde el punto de vista de la excultación y de los sistemas de control de movimientos que tiene la Generalitat sobre todos los edificios afectados que están en observación antes de la vuelta de los vecinos.

Hasta este viernes, 54 de las 87 viviendas afectadas tenían el visto bueno de los técnicos y el 38% restante había quedado a la espera de más novedades. Ahora, con el anuncio de este viernes, quedarán sin volver a corto plazo un total de 18 viviendas y siete de los 16 comercios afectados. Pero la estimación del tiempo que conlleva consolidar el terreno y, por ende, el retraso viene tras " muchas horas de inyección de cemento ". Por ello en casos como el del número 2 de la calle Rubinstein , uno de los edificios con más daños más estructurales, se necesitará un proceso de reparación aún más largo.

stories.headline: Barcelona records a new sea-temperature high of 27.9°C amid exceptional Mediterranean heat

sources.body: L’estiu 2026, no només està deixant rècords històrics de la temperatura de l’aire, amb la temperatura més alta mai registrada a la ciutat , sinó que també s’està notant amb la temperatura de l’aigua del mar . Aquesta última setmana del mes d’agost, i també de l’estiu meteorològic, el nostre observador Diego Lázaro ha informat d’un nou rècord registrat . Els 27,9 ºC registrats a un metre de fondària són la temperatura més alta registrada. Tant és així, que queda +2,4 ºC per sobre la mitjana, que és d’uns 25,5 ºC. L’arribada dels vents del nord i d’una bombolla menys càlida a uns 1.500 metres d’altura permetran que aquesta temperatura es desinfli una mica, mantenint-se però ben per sobre la mitjana les pròximes setmanes. Temperatura de l’aigua del mar a Barcelona el 2026: a quants graus es troba ara? | GRÀFICS Ariadna Corominas del Hoyo Oriol Rodríguez Ballester 2 minuts de lectura Evolució de la temperatura de l’aigua del mar a Barcelona aquest 2026 El gràfic des de l’1 de gener mostra com, des de finals d’abril, que ja va ser de rècord a escala termomètrica , la temperatura del mar ha anat pujant de manera ben accelerada, batent rècords ja al juny i juliol . De fet, l’any passat ja es van batre diversos rècords , amb l’aigua del mar del setembre més calenta en, com a mínim, els darrers 20 anys . Nous rècords en el conjunt del mediterrani Els rècords termomètrics del mar no es concentren només a Barcelona, sinó que cada dia són més extensos i intensos en el conjunt de Catalunya i el Mediterrani També et pot interessar Copernicus registra un nou rècord de la temperatura del mar: “Un oceà sota una pressió creixent” Ariadna Corominas del Hoyo 2 minuts de lectura De fet, les últimes dades marquen més de 26 ºC al Cap de Begur, més de 28 ºC a Tarragona i, amb un rècord històric registrat fa unes setmanes, gairebé 31 ºC a Sa Dragonera (al mar Balear). Amb el mapa de la temperatura de l’aigua, s’observa la gran diferència entre, l’ oceà atlàntic , que en alguns punts es troba per sota dels 20 ºC , i el mediterrani , que de mitjana supera els 28 ºC . Cal destacar, tot i així, que l’ oceà Atlàntic registra també anomalies positives aquest estiu. Com afecta això el clima? Evidentment, aquesta anomalia de la temperatura de l’aigua del mar té un impacte al clima . La relació no és directe i no està estretament lligat, però l’escalfor acumulada del mar, més els rècords que s’han anat batent aquest estiu , poden provocar que, quan arribin condicions d’ aire fred en altura , es formin greus tempestes , com ja vam viure amb els aiguats de Tarragona ara fa una setmana. A més, la funció termoreguladora que tenia el mar, que ajudava a apaivagar la forta calor dels estius i feia que la població emigrés cap a punts costaners, ha desaparegut i, fins i tot, està provocant l’efecte contrari . L’aigua del mar tan anormalment calenta ajuda que les nits siguin més càlides i que les nits tropicals i sobretot tòrrides es facin cada vegada més freqüents a la costa.

sources.body: Els bombers continuen treballant per extingir l’incendi que crema al Parc de Collserola des d’aquest dimarts i que ha cremat 54 hectàrees . Tot i que el foc ja està controlat , es continua vigilant i refredant el perímetre perquè no hi hagi revifades. “Hi ha algun punt calent a l’interior, bufa una mica més de vent i s’han activat algunes soques, però la part interior del perímetre no revesteix cap perill”, ha explicat a betevé l’ Emili Dalmau , oficial de la Unitat Tècnica del GRAF dels Bombers de la Generalitat. També et pot interessar L’incendi de Collserola, el més gran que ha patit la serra dels últims 30 anys Max Sagués 2 minuts de lectura “Ha estat un incendi atípic”, amb vent de ponent Ja fa quatre dies que es treballa a la zona, el que demostra que la feina dels bombers no ha estat fàcil. De fet, aquest ha estat l’incendi més gran a Collserola en els últims 30 anys . “ Ens haurem d’acostumar a veure aquests grans incendis més sovint del que era normal abans”, explica Dalmau. “La solució fa temps que es va donar i és evitar en la mesura del possible el canvi climàtic “, afegeix. “Ha estat un incendi atípic . No és el que majoritàriament passa aquí a Collserola”, argumenta Dalmau. Normalment en aquesta serra hi bufa la brisa marina que empeny el foc cap amunt, però quan es va declarar bufava vent de ponent . Aquest vent, a més, va obrir el flanc dret de l’incendi i el va fer córrer “més ràpid del previst “. Aquest flanc es va aconseguir apagar amb foc tècnic aprofitant una carretera, on era impossible que les flames seguissin avançant. La Generalitat mantendrá cerrado el acceso a Collserola todo el verano, tras detectar otros seis nuevos positivos de peste porcina. / EL PERIÓDICO

Por segunda vez desde el inicio del brote de peste porcina africana (PPA) en Catalunya , declarado el pasado 28 de noviembre, la Conselleria d'Agricultura de la Generalitat ha confirmado que ninguna de las 267 muestras analizadas en la última semana ha dado positivo al virus dentro de la zona de alto riesgo. La Generalitat califica la noticia de muy positiva, aunque advierte que se van a mantener durante un tiempo más las restricciones en la zona de Collserola , donde seguirán vigentes las restricciones de acceso "hasta que los científicos que marcan la estrategia para erradicar la enfermedad así lo comuniquen", han indicado fuentes del departamento que dirige el conseller Òscar Ordeig .

De hecho, en declaraciones recientes, Ordeig ha apuntado que la entrada de los ciudadanos al parque natural no se normalizará hasta posiblemente el otoño . Si en las próximas semanas siguen sin hallarse nuevos casos de la infección, se pondrá en marcha, eso sí, el calendario para que dentro de 12 meses los ganaderos que crían porcino en Catalunya y la industria cárnica puedan volver a exportar sus productos sin restricciones .

"Es imprescindible el cumplimiento de las restricciones, las medidas de bioseguridad y la colaboración de toda la ciudadanía ", han reclamado las mismas fuentes de Agricultura en conversación con este diario. Desde el inicio de esta crisis ganadera, de la que este viernes se cumplen ya nueve meses , las capturas de jabalíes en la zona infectada (zona de alto riesgo y zona de bajo riesgo) suman un total de 11.011 animales. "Lo importante es conseguir que se rebaje la densidad de la especie, para evitar que pueda haber nuevos contagios", insiste el mismo portavoz. Mientras tanto, siguen desplegados en la zona más de un millar de efectivos de los Agents Rurals y Mossos d'Esquadra, las sociedades de cazadores, el Grupo Especial de Prevención de Incendios Forestales (GEPIF), además de 36 trampas y 94 'pig brigs' (trampas colectivas) y para evitar la salida o entrada de jabalíes dentro de las zonas restringidas se han ejecutado 353 cierres perimetrales.

stories.headline: Barcelona plans an additional €150 million for blue-economy projects through 2030

sources.body:
Acto de colocación de la primera piedra del BlueTechPort / BLUETECHPORT / VÍDEO: QUIM VALLÈS / ACN

En el contexto de su estrategia de promoción económica con el horizonte del año 2030, el Ayuntamiento de Barcelona ha anunciado una inversión de 150 millones de euros en nuevos proyectos de economía azul. Se trata de una inyección económica de unos 50 millones más que la del 2021-2025, que ha implicado inversiones de más de 98 millones de euros en infraestructuras "que han consolidado a la ciudad como referente emergente en este ámbito", asegura el consistorio.

La concreción de la inversión anunciada por el consistorio pasará por la consolidación del Parc de Tecnologia Marítima de Barcelona, el BlueTechPort o Barcelona Mar de Ciència, que implicarán 146 de los millones presupuestados. Los otros 4 millones se destinarán a programas de impulso de la actividad y emprendimiento. Además, el presupuesto inicial puede recibir hasta 75 millones de euros adicionales procedentes de Barcelona Investment Fund o el programa Ports 4.0.

"Barcelona reafirma su apuesta por la economía azul como un sector estratégico para generar ocupación de calidad, innovación y actividad económica vinculada al mar", ha subrayado la quinta tenienta de Alcaldía de Barcelona, Raquel Gil, también presidenta de la agencia municipal de desarrollo económico Barcelona Activa.

La nueva hoja de ruta busca reforzar el papel del litoral como eje de desarrollo económico a través de tres ejes: incorporar el agua dulce; ampliar el impacto internacional de los proyectos; y corresponsabilizar en este ecosistema a otros actores en la línea de colaboración público-privada. La incorporación de proyectos orientados al agua dulce responde a la necesidad de mejorar la gestión de los recursos hídricos frente a la situación de sequía y de inundaciones. La estrategia incluye iniciativas como el despliegue de sistemas urbanos de drenaje sostenible, proyectos de reutilización de aguas o actuaciones para optimizar el ciclo del agua en Barcelona, así como el programa de emprendimiento B-Blue, que incorpora el agua dulce como nueva línea de innovación.

La búsqueda del mayor impacto de los proyectos supondrá el refuerzo de las infraestructuras de la ciudad, "que sumarán nuevos espacios en el litoral destinados a la investigación, la innovación y el emprendimiento, y facilitarán la implantación de empresas y proyectos de alto valor añadido vinculados al mar", asegura un comunicado municipal.

La proyección internacional del plan se materializa en proyectos que sitúan a Barcelona en el escenario global de la economía azul. Es el caso del Ocean Decade Collaborative Centre (DCC) en Barcelona, el centro global de la UNESCO dedicado a desarrollar una economía oceánica sostenible, "que situará a la ciudad como nodo de referencia internacional para la generación de conocimiento y la conexión de proyectos en este ámbito", explica el consistorio. El proyecto se desarrolla en alianza con el Port de Barcelona, la Generalitat de Catalunya y agentes de conocimiento como el Instituto de Ciencias del Mar (ICM-CSIC) o BlueNetCat, con la Fundación Barcelona Capital Náutica como entidad implementadora.
